results.title: Queen Marie of Romania by Frederic Storck
results.description:
This patinated terracotta bust portrays Queen Marie of Romania with a refined elegance characteristic of Frederic Storck’s mature sculptural style. The artist captures the queen’s noble presence through a harmonious balance of realism and idealization, emphasizing both her strength and her grace. Queen Marie’s face is modeled with soft yet well‑defined features: a calm, introspective expression, gently arched eyebrows, and a composed gaze that projects dignity. Her hair is arranged in broad, stylized waves, a hallmark of her iconic appearance in early 20th‑century portraiture.
The bust was made in the first quarter of the 20th century.
Today, the work is preserved and exhibited at the Frederic Storck and Cecilia Cuțescu‑Storck Museum, a historic house museum dedicated to the artistic legacy of the Storck family.

results.title: Chelys Lyre Reconstruction Lefkada
results.description:
Recreation of an ancient chelys (tortoise-shell) lyre: a real turtle-shell helonio with bone tuning keys—found in Lefkada tombs—and re-strung with goat-horn arms and a notched yoke by local craftsman Giorgos Polyzos. The set is exhibited in Hall I of the Archaeological Museum of Lefkada, Lefkada Town, Ionian Islands, Greece (38.8350 N / 20.7040 E).

Chelys lyres were light, portable bowl-lyres used across Classical and early Hellenistic Greece; a similar instrument is described in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, where the god fashions the first lyre from a tortoise shell and horn uprights.

 Typical examples had 7–9 gut strings and were played by both men and women; their compact body made them ideal for musical training.

results.title: Marble Bull – Votive of Regilla at Olympia
results.description: Carved in Pentelic marble around AD 160–170, this life-size bull once decorated the grand nymphaeum (monumental fountain) built by the Roman aristocrat Appia Annia Regilla inside the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia. A Greek dedicatory inscription on both flanks records her offering “to Zeus” and secures the find-spot and patronage. The animal strides forward with a lowered head, its dynamic pose balanced today on a modern support where the original legs were lost. Excavated in 1892 among the nymphaeum’s collapsed marble revetments, it illustrates the lavish benefactions of Herodes Atticus and Regilla and the fusion of Roman wealth with Greek religious tradition. Now exhibited in the Archaeological Museum of Olympia.

results.title: Inchbofin, Co. Westmeath (WM015-001009)
results.description:
National Monuments Service Description: a three-lined looped cross with enlarged centre and ends. The centre of the slab is occupied by a curved swastika or tetraskelion, the arms of which turn sunwise. The loops at the corners of both stones turn in the same direction as the swastika. In most crosses with loops the latter are symmetrical, and do not follow in one direction as here. All the expanded ends contain frets. In this they follow the Clonmacnois patterns. In slab (C) the top and dexter arm show one pattern and the base and sinister arm another, while in (D) all are alike. There are no inscriptions. results.title: Wmid-7a7bfb Medieval Cooking Vessel Leg
results.description:
An incomplete copper alloy foot / leg from a copper alloy cooking vessel of Late Medieval to Early Post Medieval dating (AD 1400 - AD 1700).

The vessel fragment is sub rectangular in plan and sub triangular in cross section. The vessel leg has a flared terminal, probably imitating an animal paw. A horizontal ridge is located above the flared terminal. The interior surface is flat. Both the top and base have been broken at an angle and exhibits a rough, uneven surface.

The remains of copper alloy cooking vessels have been regularly recorded through the PAS, with many variants on the design. This leg was probably originally part of a cauldron, suggestive by the ridge on the exterior.

results.title: Magpie Goose (Wetland Grazer of Australasia)
results.description:
This voxel-style model represents the Magpie Goose (Anseranas semipalmata), a distinctive Australian waterbird known for its striking black-and-white plumage and elongated neck. With its broad chest, orange legs, and pronounced bill, this stylized model captures the bird’s elegant yet sturdy form. The minimalist, blocky design makes it ideal for educational 3D exhibits and wildlife-inspired voxel environments.

Geographic Distribution & Habitat

The Magpie Goose is native to northern and eastern Australia and southern New Guinea. It inhabits floodplains, freshwater wetlands, and tropical marshes, often nesting in large colonies during the wet season. The species feeds on aquatic vegetation, seeds, and tubers, contributing to wetland ecosystem dynamics as both grazer and seed disperser.
